paper_title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

Across 166M1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.82.0% over GDN-2 and 2.53.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560 from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2 faster, and training 2.7 faster than Transformer at 32K. 1. Introduction As large language models scale to long-document comprehension, multi-hop reasoning, and in-context retrieval, the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) faces fundamental scaling bottleneck: softmax selfattention requires training compute that grows quadratically with sequence length and an inference cache that grows linearly. Linear attention removes this bottleneck by compressing variable-length context into fixed-size key-value state, enabling linear-time training and constant-memory inference (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Choromanski et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2021; Orvieto et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023; Gu and Dao, 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Dao and Gu, 2024; De et al., 2024). However, because finite-dimensional state admits only finitely many orthogonal key directions, packing more keys into the state forces cross-key interference (Johnson and Lindenstrauss, 1984; Smolensky, 1990; Arora et al., 2023a; Jelassi et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024a). Delta-rule recurrences (Widrow and Hoff, 1960; Schlag et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024; Grazzi et al., 2024; Siems et al., 2025) mitigate this interference by erasing the current prediction for an incoming key before writing new value. In particular, Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025b) pairs scalar exponential decay with delta-rule erasure, Kimi Linear (Kimi Team et al., 2025) introduces channel-wise decay so state rows evolve at independent rates, and Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) generalizes both by decoupling erasure and writes into channel-wise gates so each state row and value channel updates independently. Parameterizing decay, erasure, and writes with channel-wise gates, however, introduces three bottlenecks across parameter allocation, state readout, and parallel training. First, when decoupling erasure and writes per channel, GDN-2 treats both gates symmetrically, allocating full-rank 𝑑 𝑑 projections to each while compressing the decay and output gates through low-rank bottlenecks; these two full-rank matrices alone consume 2𝑑2 parameters (one-sixth of the 12𝑑2 layer budget), so the gates together shrink the feed-forward network (FFN) width by over 25% to remain iso-parameter with Transformer. Second, because state rows decay at different rates, slow-decaying rows accumulate value writes over hundreds to thousands of tokens while Corresponding author(s): cjsschaefer@google.com. Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout Figure 1 Muir outperforms GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and long-context throughput while improving recall over GDN-2. (a) Sensitivity-allocated low-rank gates with FFN expansion drive the bulk of the validation NLL gain over GDN-2, while dynamic matched-filter readout drives the gain on extractive recall. (b) Across 166M1.34B parameters, Muir lowers validation NLL by 18.020.4 millinats over GDN-2 and 25.036.2 millinats over Transformer. (c) On 8 TPU7x chips (0.5M tokens/step) at 1.34B with our chunkwise kernel, Muir matches GDN-2 throughput despite an additional readout gate and 30.4% wider FFN, and trains 1.64 and 2.74 faster than Transformer at 16K and 32K, respectively. fast-decaying rows retain only recent inputs, so state row norms span more than an order of magnitude. Under unweighted query readout, high-norm slow rows dominate the output and force stronger write-time erasure to suppress their interference, which prematurely overwrites stored associations. Third, because channels decay at independent rates, chunkwise parallel training (Sun et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; 2024; 2025b) must divide keys by cumulative decay prefixes to compute within-chunk interactions via matrix multiplication and solve lower-triangular system per chunk, which breaks down on wide-matrix-unit accelerators. While GPU kernels (Yang and Zhang, 2024; Kimi Team et al., 2025) avoid full-chunk division and solve diagonal triangular sub-blocks sequentially in SRAM at small chunks matched to 16 16 TensorCores, accelerators that pair wide systolic matrix units with much slower vector unit (such as AWS Trainium and Google TPUs, reaching 256 256 matrix units with vector units over 60 slower on modern TPUs; Austin et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026) require large chunks for high matrix utilization. At these chunk sizes, cumulative decay prefixes underflow on fast-decaying channels and overflow the division; alternatively, materializing pairwise channel decays or solving the triangular system sequentially falls back to the slow vector unit. To address these challenges, we analyze channel-wise gated delta recurrences and show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: rectifying key activations (such as SiLU; Ramachandran et al., 2018) and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate requires much lower-rank projection than the write gate. We further derive closed-form scaling law for state row norms and show that weighting queries by matched-filter readout gain balances row contributions, which lowers the write-time erasure needed to suppress interference and extends the memory horizon. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, gated delta-rule model that fuses all recurrence and output gates into sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, modulates queries with matched-filter readout gate (combining static channel profile with dynamic per-token modulation) to re-weight state rows, and reinvests the saved gate parameters under fixed budget to widen the FFN and expand its capacity for factual associations (Geva et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022). Finally, to train stably at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design boundary-pivoted chunkwise kernel that splits relative decays without division or full-chunk 3D decay tensors and solves within-chunk triangular systems via block matrix multiplications. Figure 1 summarizes our main findings. Across model scales from 166M to 1.34B parameters, Muir outperforms both GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and commonsense reasoning, and improves over GDN-2 on real-world extractive recall (Arora et al., 2024a;b). At 1.34B, Muir improves synthetic multi-hop and multi-needle retrieval (Hsieh et al., 2024) over both baselines, and extrapolates from 4K to 10M-token streams in 25 MB float32 state without perplexity drift, whereas Dynamic YaRN Transformer (Peng et al., 2024) diverges past 8K and needs 2.1 TB bfloat16 KV cache at 10M. On passkey retrieval, our static matchedfilter readout achieves near-100% accuracy to 1M tokens, whereas GDN-2 collapses past 4K8K. Using our chunkwise kernel for both recurrent models and Splash Attention (TPU implementation of FlashAttention; 2 Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023) for Transformer, Muir matches GDN-2 training throughput across sequence lengths despite wider FFN and an additional gate, reaches the 100B-token validation loss of GDN-2 1.2 faster, and trains 2.7 faster than Transformer at 32K. Mechanistic analysis confirms that state updates are more sensitive to writes than to erasure; state row norms closely follow our scaling law; and the learned readout balances state rows, lowers write-time erasure, and retains associations over longer contexts. 2. Experimental Setup Models and Baselines. We evaluate all models across four iso-parameter scales: 166M (𝐿 = 8, 𝑑 = 1,024), 406M (𝐿 = 11, 𝑑 = 1,536), 834M (𝐿 = 14, 𝑑 = 2,048), and 1.34B (𝐿 = 24, 𝑑 = 2,048), where all architectures at given scale share depth 𝐿, residual width 𝑑, head dimension 𝑑𝑘 = 𝑑𝑣 = 128 (𝑁ℎ = 𝑑/128 heads), GELU FFN, and untied input and output embeddings (full per-scale configurations are provided in Appendix G.1). Under the 12𝑑2 per-layer non-embedding parameter budget, we compare five model variants across all four scales: (i) Transformer, with rotary position embeddings (RoPE, 𝜃 = 10,000; Su et al., 2021), FFN width 𝑑ffn = 4𝑑, and TPU Pallas Splash Attention (Dao et al., 2022);4 (ii) GDN-2, the channel-wise gated delta recurrence with rank-128 (𝑓, 𝑔) gates, dense 𝑑 𝑑 (𝑏, 𝑤) gates, and 𝑑ffn = 3𝑑 256;5 (iii) Muir (no 𝛾), which replaces the gate projections in GDN-2 with the fused low-rank projection of ranks (𝑟𝑓 , 𝑟𝑏, 𝑟𝑔, 𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (64, 64, 128, 256, 0) and unit readout (𝛾𝑡 = 1); (iv) Muir (static 𝛾), which adds the learned static readout gain 𝛾𝑡 = 𝛾stat at the same gate ranks; and (v) Muir (ours), which splits the 256-column write budget into (𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (128, 128) to parameterize the dynamic readout gain 𝛾𝑡. Depth Horizon and Real-World Extractive Recall. In the depth-by-length breakdown (Figure 6e), both GDN-2 and Muir maintain uniform recall across needle depths at 1K2K (with Muir leading by 712 points), whereas decoupling query-time noise suppression from write-time erasure (Proposition 3.10) prevents the premature overwriting that causes GDN-2 accuracy to drop sharply on early-context needles (040% depth) at 4K8K. Similarly, on Based/JRT (Figure 6f), extracting semi-structured attributes (SWDE, FDA) and passage spans (SQuAD, TriviaQA, NQ, DROP) from natural documents requires resolving query-target lags that vary widely across examples. Consequently, FFN expansion (Muir no 𝛾) and static scaling (Muir static 𝛾) yield only modest gains over GDN-2, whereas dynamic 𝛾𝑡 adapts the channel filter per query token to drive the bulk of the six-task improvement and surpass Transformer on DROP. 5.2.3. When readout gain is omitted or static (𝑟𝑞 = 0), four uniform rank-128 gates (128, 128, 128, 128, 0) sum to 𝑅tot = 512 and perform comparably to the sensitivityallocated (64, 64, 128, 256, 0) variants across scales. To separate the effect of low-rank gating from FFN expansion under the 12𝑑2 budget, we vary gate ranks and FFN width independently at 406M relative to GDN-2 (𝑑ffn = 4,352). Lower write-time erasure (Proposition 3.10) raises retention in Muir at 𝑡q over GDN-2 from 37% to 45% on 𝐻1 and from 46% to 52% on average across 𝐻1𝐻5 (Figure 13c,d). Across 𝐴1𝐴4, dynamic 𝛾𝑡 shifts the channel filter (Proposition 3.6) so ^𝑞𝑡𝑆𝑡 concentrates weight along the target diagonal 𝐻1𝐻4, most notably on the oldest root hop (18% to 23% at 𝐴1; Figure 13e). 7. Conclusion Channel-wise gates give delta-rule models fine-grained control over fixed-size state, but its effective capacity depends on the state dynamics those gates induce. In our trained models, key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto roughly 5% of channels per head, making the state 13 more sensitive to write than to erase perturbations; Muir therefore fuses all gates into low-rank projection with smaller decay and erase bottlenecks, widening the FFN by up to 30.4% at fixed parameters and FLOPs. Meanwhile, consistent with our theory, multi-timescale decay drives state row-energy variation across orders of magnitude, exceeding 100 in heads mixing fast and slow channels. Compared to GDN-2, Muir reduces median readout-energy spread by 35% and write-time erasure by 17%, improves root-needle multi-hop retention from 37% to 45%, and lowers the median condition number of the chunkwise triangular solve by 24%. Our results also reveal two remaining limitations. First, under fixed gate-rank budget, static and dynamic readout trade single-horizon retention against multi-lag adaptability. On passkey lookup, static filter suffices for single query lag and preserves write rank for near-perfect recall to 1M tokens, whereas halving write rank to fund dynamic readout limits single-needle retention beyond 32K. Conversely, static readout cannot match varying lags on multi-hop and extractive tasks, and drifts on continuous text as slow-row energy accumulates, whereas dynamic readout adapts per token to resolve multi-lag queries and hold flat perplexity across 10M-token streams. Second, while our pure-JAX kernel matches GDN-2 throughput and trains 2.74 faster than Transformer at 32K, Splash Attention remains faster at short contexts (< 11K) because its Pallas 24 Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout kernel fuses masking and block contractions in VMEM while XLA materializes chunk temporaries in HBM. These limitations suggest several directions for future work. Parameterizing dynamic readout through our analytical matched filter by predicting one lag per head and tracking expected row energy could unify distant passkey recall, multi-lag routing, and stream stability without sacrificing write rank. Alternatively, pairing sliding-window attention with static-readout Muir would resolve this tension architecturally: local attention copies nearby spans exactly in constant memory, freeing the recurrent state to keep full write rank for distant lookup without periodic global attention or growing KV cache. At the kernel level, fusing leaf Neumann inversion, the boundary-pivoted merge tree, and the cross-chunk state scan into single Pallas kernel would keep chunk temporaries in VMEM and narrow the short-context throughput gap. Beyond gated delta recurrences, sensitivity-allocated gating and matched-filter readout extend to matrix-state test-time optimization models whose channels decay or update at different rates under unweighted queries.

Additional Related Work Linear Attention, State-Space Models, and Fast-Weight Memories. Replacing the 𝒪(𝑇 ) key-value cache and 𝒪(𝑇 2) attention matrix of softmax attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) with fixed-size associative state matrix has roots in Hopfield networks (Hopfield, 1982) and fast-weight controllers (Schmidhuber, 1992; Ba et al., 2016). Kernelized linear transformers (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Choromanski et al., 2020; Pham and Pagh, 2013; Kacham et al., 2024; Ghriss and Chakraborty, 2026) factorize the attention kernel into feature maps so that causal sequence mixing reduces to an additive outer-product recurrence 𝑆𝑡 = 𝑆𝑡1 + 𝑘 𝑡 𝑣𝑡, but purely additive accumulation suffers from unbounded state growth and associative cross-talk once sequence length exceeds the key dimension (Schlag et al., 2021; Arora et al., 2023a; Jelassi et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024a;b). Structured state-space models (SSMs), long-convolution architectures, and fixed-decay linear recurrences such as S4 (Gu et al., 2021), BiGS (Wang et al., 2023), H3 (Fu et al., 2022), Hyena (Poli et al., 2023), LRU (Orvieto et al., 2023), RWKV (Peng et al., 2023), and RetNet (Sun et al., 2023) introduce data-independent exponential decay across state channels or heads, while selective SSMs and gated linear recurrences, including Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023), Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024), Gated Attention Unit (FLASH; Hua et al., 2022), Griffin (De et al., 2024), HGRN (Qin et al., 2023), HGRN2 (Qin et al., 2024b), xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024), Gated Linear Attention (GLA; Yang et al., 2023), Gated Slot Attention (GSA; Zhang et al., 2024), ReGLA (Lu et al., 2025), and Mamba-3 (Lahoti et al., 2026), make decay gates data-dependent so the model can selectively forget stale context (van der Westhuizen and Lasenby, 2018; Sun et al., 2025). Although data-dependent exponential decay bounds the total state norm, diagonal decay scales an entire state channel uniformly and cannot selectively erase single key-value association without flushing other associations stored along the same channel (Yang et al., 2024; 2025b). Delta-Rule Recurrences and Online Test-Time Optimization. To support targeted associative updates, Fast Weight Programmers (Schlag et al., 2021) and DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024) replace additive writes with the Widrow-Hoff delta rule (Widrow and Hoff, 1960), which subtracts the current state prediction 𝑘𝑡𝑆𝑡1 along key 𝑘𝑡 prior to writing the new value. Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025b) combines scalar exponential decay with scalar Householder-like delta transition; more broadly, selective SSMs and gated linear recurrences are widely interleaved with softmax attention in hybrid sequence models (Ren et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025; Lenz et al., 2025; MiniMax et al., 2025; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026). Subsequent extensions introduce vector or matrix-valued erasure and decay in RWKV-7 (Peng et al., 2025), Kimi Linear (KDA; Kimi Team et al., 2025), and GDN-2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026), cross-layer value and residual routing in Cerruti et al. (2026), multi-step or negative-eigenvalue state transitions in Grazzi et al. (2024), DeltaProduct (Siems et al., 2025), and Comba (Hu et al., 2025), non-linear matrix-state transitions in M2RNN (Mishra et al., 2026b), sparse slot-addressed state expansion in Sparse Delta Memory (Cabannes et al., 2026), and hierarchical or higher-order recurrent states in Log-Linear Attention (Guo et al., 2026) and Triadic Linear Attention (Sieberling et al., 2026). parallel line of work interprets these recurrences as online test-time optimization of an internal regression or associative memory objective: Test-Time Training (TTT; Sun et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026), Longhorn (Liu et al., 2024), Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025c), ATLAS (Behrouz et al., 2025a), Miras (Behrouz et al., 2025b), Test-Time Regression (Wang et al., 2025), MesaNet (von Oswald et al., 2025), Lattice (Karami et al., 2025), Gated KalmaNet (Peng et al., 2026), Kaczmarz Linear Attention (Zou et al., 2026), and Momentum Delta Networks (Huang et al., 2026) derive recurrent state updates as single-step gradient, momentum, Kaczmarz, Newton, or Kalman updates on key-value reconstruction loss (see Appendix for the optimization lens). Across these architectures, KDA (Kimi Team et al., 2025) and RWKV-7 (Peng et al., 2025) retain 4𝑑 FFN by avoiding dense 𝑑 𝑑 recurrence gates: KDA restricts key erasure and value writes to shared per-head scalar alongside low-rank decay and output gates, while RWKV-7 uses low-rank decay, removal, value-residual, and output gates with decoupled removal and replacement keys. By contrast, GDN-2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) decouples channelwise erasure and writes on shared key via dense 𝑑𝑑 projections at the expense of FFN width (Shazeer, 2020; Geva et al., 2021). For state readout, whereas query-key normalized attention (Hua et al., 2022; Dehghani et al., 2023) and diagonal SSMs (Lahoti et al., 2026) apply learned per-channel gains to both queries and keys after normalization, delta-rule recurrences require unit-norm keys (𝑘𝑡2 = 1) to keep rank-one erasure contractive and therefore evaluate the unweighted product 𝑜𝑡 = 𝑞𝑡𝑆𝑡 (or scalar per-head rescaling; Hu et al., 2025) after parameter-free ℓ2 normalization (Henry et al., 2020; Schlag et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024) and post-readout gating (Qiu et al., 2025). Recent test-time optimization models instead precondition queries via running key-covariance state (von Oswald et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026; Le et al., 2026) or orthogonalize 𝑆𝑡 via Newton-Schulz iterations during training (Aquino-Michaels, 2026). Our analysis in 3 shows that state updates are much more sensitive to write-gate than to erase-gate perturbations (Proposition 3.1), allowing all five gates to share low-rank bottleneck, and that diagonal matched-filter readout 𝑜𝑡 = (𝛾𝑡 𝑞𝑡)𝑆𝑡 corrects 36 Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout the row-energy imbalance of channel-wise decay (Propositions 3.4, 3.6 and 3.10) without covariance state or matrix orthogonalization. Hardware-Efficient Chunkwise Algorithms. Executing token-level matrix recurrences efficiently on modern accelerators requires reformulating sequential outer products into block-parallel matrix multiplications (Blelloch, 1989; Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023; Shah et al., 2024). For diagonal decay recurrences, FLASH (Hua et al., 2022), RetNet (Sun et al., 2023), GLA (Yang et al., 2023), Lightning Attention-2 (Qin et al., 2024a), Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024; Santoni, 2026), FLA (Yang and Zhang, 2024), and Tiled Flash Linear Attention (Beck et al., 2025) partition the sequence into chunks of length 𝐶, compute within-chunk outputs via masked matrix-matrix multiplications, and propagate the state across chunk boundaries. When ^𝑘𝑡, unrolling chunk of 𝐶 transitions yields product the state transition includes rank-one key erasure 𝑘 𝑡 of 𝐶 rank-one perturbations. DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024) and Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025b) compact this product using the classical WY representation of Householder transformations (Bischof and Van Loan, 1987; Schreiber and Van Loan, 1989; Joffrain et al., 2006), which reduces within-chunk parallelization to solving 𝐶 𝐶 unit lower-triangular system 𝑇 = + 𝐿strict. On GPUs, FLA (Yang and Zhang, 2024) and KDA (Kimi Team et al., 2025) subdivide each 𝐶 = 64 chunk into 16-token sub-chunks (Yang et al., 2023), compute decays relative to sub-chunk boundaries instead of dividing by full-chunk prefixes, invert the four diagonal 16 16 blocks sequentially in SRAM, and merge off-diagonal 16 16 blocks on TensorCores. On TPUs, however, the matrix multiply unit (MXU) is 256 256 systolic array while the vector processing unit (VPU) is over 60 slower in bfloat16 (Austin et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026), so 16 16 tiles under-utilize the MXU and sequential leaf substitution stalls on the VPU. Concurrent work on FLAT (Mishra et al., 2026a) provides hand-tuned Pallas TPU kernels for diagonal-decay recurrences (Linear Attention, Mamba-2, GLA) without the delta-rule triangular solve; FlyWheel (Bao et al., 2026) develops Pallas TPU kernels for softmax attention and for Gated DeltaNet inference via MXU triangular inversion; and Sobczyk et al. (2026) benchmark matrix-product-rich triangular inversion (including hybrid leaf-Neumann and recursive block-merge forward kernels) on an already-materialized 𝑇 on GPUs and NPUs. In 4.2, rather than materializing 𝑇 upfront via prefix division, we form cross-blocks via boundary-pivoted log-decay splitting at each merge step of recursive block-Neumann inversion (Heller, 1974; Orcutt, 1974; Heller, 1978; Bini and Pan, 1994; Sobczyk et al., 2026) and differentiate the solve in two full-chunk GEMMs with on-the-fly VMEM pivot recomputation, routing 98% of 𝐶 = 256 training FLOPs onto 256 256 MXU contractions. 37 Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout B. Language Modeling and Commonsense Reasoning All perplexity and zero-shot commonsense evaluations in Tables 1 and 2 are executed via the lm-evaluationharness (v0.4.11; Gao et al., 2024) with float32 output logits, rolling log-likelihood context window 2,048 (and 4,096 in Table 12) for WikiText, and length-normalized accuracy (acc n) for HellaSwag and ARCChallenge (Yang et al., 2025b; Lahoti et al., 2026).
